# Jonah Chapter 3 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 340v–341r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/JON_003_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Then the LORD spoke to Jonah a second time: **2** "Get up and go to the great city of Nineveh. Deliver the message I give you."

**3** This time Jonah obeyed and went to Nineveh as the LORD had commanded. Now Nineveh was an enormous city — it took three days to walk through it. **4** On the first day of his walk through the city, Jonah shouted his message: "Forty days from now, Nineveh will be destroyed!"

**5** The people of Nineveh believed God's message. They declared a fast, and everyone from the most important to the least important put on sackcloth to show their sorrow.

**6** When the king of Nineveh heard what was happening, he got up from his throne, took off his royal robes, dressed himself in sackcloth, and sat in ashes. **7** He sent out this decree throughout the city: "By order of the king and his officials: No person or animal, no herd or flock, may eat or drink anything. **8** Every person and animal must be covered in sackcloth. Everyone must cry out to God with all their heart. Everyone must turn from their evil ways and stop their violence. **9** Who knows? Perhaps God will change his mind and hold back his fierce anger. Perhaps we will not be destroyed."

**10** When God saw that they had abandoned their evil ways, he changed his mind. He did not carry out the destruction he had threatened.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The five-word sermon (v.4):** In Hebrew, Jonah's entire message is just five words: *od arba'im yom ve-Nineveh nehpakhet*. It is the shortest, most reluctant prophetic sermon ever delivered — no call to repentance, no offer of mercy, just a countdown to destruction. And yet it works. The Ninevites hear judgment and choose to repent anyway — without being invited to.

**Animals in sackcloth (vv.7-8):** The king orders even the livestock to fast and wear sackcloth. This detail is often read as comic — absurd, over-the-top repentance. But it may reflect actual ancient Near Eastern mourning practice. More importantly, it shows total, whole-creation repentance — a sharp contrast to Jonah's total, whole-being resistance.

**"Who knows?" (v.9):** The most theologically honest two words in the book. The king of Nineveh makes no presumption that God must respond to repentance. He merely hopes. And that vulnerable hope — without guarantee or entitlement — is exactly what moves God to act.

*— PNEUMA*
